solution: \(d(P,Q) = |3 - (-5)| = 8\), \(d(Q,R) = |-5 - 6| = 11\), \(d(P,R) = |3 - 6| = 3\). So \(d(P,Q) + d(Q,R) = 8 + 11 = 19\), which is not equal to \(d(P,R) = 3\). (Q does not lie between P and R.) The statement is False.

\(d(P,R) = |3 - 6| = 3\), \(d(R,Q) = |6 - (-5)| = 11\), \(d(P,Q) = |3 - (-5)| = 8\). So \(d(P,R) + d(R,Q) = 3 + 11 = 14\), which is not equal to \(d(P,Q) = 8\). (R does not lie between P and Q.) The statement is False.

\(d(R,P) = |6 - 3| = 3\), \(d(P,Q) = |3 - (-5)| = 8\), \(d(R,Q) = |6 - (-5)| = 11\). So \(d(R,P) + d(P,Q) = 3 + 8 = 11 = d(R,Q)\). This holds because \(-5 < 3 < 6\), so P lies between R and Q, that is \(R\text{-}P\text{-}Q\). The statement is True.
\(d(P,Q) = |3 - (-5)| = 8\), \(d(P,R) = |3 - 6| = 3\), \(d(Q,R) = |-5 - 6| = 11\). So \(d(P,Q) - d(P,R) = 8 - 3 = 5\), which is not equal to \(d(Q,R) = 11\). The statement is False.

A point \(8\) units from P lies either \(8\) units to the right of P or \(8\) units to the left of P. To the right: \(-7 + 8 = 1\). To the left: \(-7 - 8 = -15\). The required co-ordinates are \(-15\) and \(1\).
Since \(A\text{-}B\text{-}C\), B lies between A and C, so \(d(A,B) + d(B,C) = d(A,C)\). Then \(d(A,B) = 17 - 6.5 = 10.5\). So \(d(A,B) = 10.5\).
Since \(P\text{-}Q\text{-}R\), Q lies between P and R, so \(d(P,R) = d(P,Q) + d(Q,R) = 3.4 + 5.7 = 9.1\). So \(d(P,R) = 9.1\).

A point \(7\) units from A lies either \(7\) units to the right of A or \(7\) units to the left of A. To the right: \(1 + 7 = 8\). To the left: \(1 - 7 = -6\). The required co-ordinates are \(-6\) and \(8\).

solution: If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary.
If a figure is a triangle, then it is formed by three segments.
If a number has only two divisors, then it is called a prime number.
If a figure is a triangle, then the sum of the measures of its angles is \(180^\circ\).
If two angles are complements of each other, then the sum of their measures is \(90^\circ\).
If two lines are parallel, then the corresponding angles formed by their transversal are congruent.
If a number is divisible by 3, then the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
Antecedent (given): All sides of a triangle are congruent. Consequent (to be proved): All angles of that triangle are congruent.

In conditional form: If two triangles are equilateral, then they are similar. Figure: draw two equilateral triangles of clearly different sizes, \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle PQR\); mark all three sides of \(\triangle ABC\) with a single tick each and all three sides of \(\triangle PQR\) with a double tick each, showing that each triangle is equilateral. Antecedent (given): \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle PQR\) are equilateral triangles. Consequent (to be proved): \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle PQR\) are similar.
diagramNote: Two separate equilateral triangles of clearly different sizes, labelled A, B, C and P, Q, R. All three sides of triangle ABC carry one tick each; all three sides of triangle PQR carry two ticks each. The tick style differs between the triangles because they are similar, not congruent.

solution: Figure: draw line AB with point C on it so that \(A\text{-}C\text{-}B\), and draw ray CD from C on one side of the line. Then \(\angle ACD\) and \(\angle DCB\) form a linear pair; mark them with equal arcs to show \(\angle ACD \cong \angle DCB\), and mark a right-angle symbol at each. Antecedent (given): \(\angle ACD\) and \(\angle DCB\) form a linear pair and \(\angle ACD \cong \angle DCB\). Consequent (to be proved): each of \(\angle ACD\) and \(\angle DCB\) measures \(90^\circ\), that is, each of them is a right angle.
diagramNote: A horizontal line AB with C between A and B; ray CD drawn upward from C. The two angles ACD and DCB each marked with a single equal arc to show congruence, and each carrying a small right-angle square at C.

solution: Figure: draw \(\triangle ABC\). From B draw the altitude on side AC, meeting AC at P, so \(\text{seg } BP \perp \text{side } AC\); from C draw the altitude on side AB, meeting AB at Q, so \(\text{seg } CQ \perp \text{side } AB\). Mark right angles at P and at Q, and mark \(\text{seg } BP\) and \(\text{seg } CQ\) with a single tick each to show \(\text{seg } BP \cong \text{seg } CQ\); mark side AB and side AC with a double tick each. Antecedent (given): In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\text{seg } BP \perp \text{side } AC\), \(\text{seg } CQ \perp \text{side } AB\) and \(\text{seg } BP \cong \text{seg } CQ\). Consequent (to be proved): \(\text{side } AC \cong \text{side } AB\).
diagramNote: Triangle ABC with two altitudes drawn: BP from vertex B perpendicular to side AC (foot P on AC) and CQ from vertex C perpendicular to side AB (foot Q on AB). Right-angle squares at P and Q. Segments BP and CQ each carry one tick (congruent altitudes); sides AB and AC each carry two ticks (the conclusion).
